subject: pritzker

brief.inclusion: Hyatt heir and two-term Democratic governor of Illinois seeking a third term in November 2026, who has put more than $326 million of his own money into his campaigns, funds Democratic causes nationally, and fought the Trump administration's 2025 National Guard deployment to the Supreme Court.
brief.namesakes: FEC records contain many Pritzkers: Jay A. (his uncle, Hyatt founder), Thomas J., Nicholas J., John A. and Penny. The subject files as Jay Robert, Jay R. or JB Pritzker. Worldview has two entities for him: "J. B. Pritzker" (OpenStates, the governor record, used here) and a duplicate "JB Pritzker" (scaffold-cycle) that should be merged.

summary: Heir to the Hyatt hotel fortune and private-equity investor who has been governor of Illinois since 2019, after spending $171.5 million of his own money to unseat Bruce Rauner; across three campaigns his self-funding exceeds $326 million. He has also given about $29 million in itemized federal contributions, including $9.75 million to the pro-Clinton super PAC in 2016 and $10 million in 2026 to back his lieutenant governor's Senate run. A leading Trump antagonist and possible 2028 presidential candidate, he is seeking a rare third term against Darren Bailey.

chapters.title: A Hyatt heir in Democratic politics
chapters.dek: A family fortune, a failed House race, and decades as a donor.
chapters.body:
Pritzker was born in Palo Alto on January 19, 1965, into the family that built the Hyatt hotel chain; his uncle Jay founded it and his father, Donald, developed it [[wikipedia, forbes-profile]]. After his father's death in 1972 he moved at 12 to Chicago to live with Jay and Cindy Pritzker. He graduated from Duke in 1987 and Northwestern law school in 1993, and co-founded the private-equity firm Pritzker Group with his brother Anthony [[wikipedia, forbes-profile]]. His sister Penny Pritzker was Obama's commerce secretary [[forbes-profile]].

His first campaign, for an open House seat in 1998, ended in a third-place finish with 20.5 percent despite nearly $1 million of his own money [[wikipedia]]. He became instead a major Democratic donor and organizer: national co-chair of Hillary Clinton's 2008 campaign and, in 2016, a donor of more than $17.5 million to her campaign and super PAC, including $9.75 million in itemized gifts to Priorities USA Action [[wikipedia, fec-pritzker]]. He chaired the creation of the Illinois Holocaust Museum, opened in 2009, and in 2015 gave $100 million to Northwestern's law school [[wikipedia]].

chapters.title: Buying a governorship, and using it
chapters.dek: A $171.5 million campaign and a progressive agenda in Springfield.
chapters.body:
Pritzker spent $171.5 million of his own money in 2018 to unseat Republican Gov. Bruce Rauner, winning 54.5 to 38.8 percent [[wikipedia]]. His first year produced a $15 minimum wage, legal recreational cannabis with pardons for about 11,000 low-level convictions, the Reproductive Health Act and a $45 billion capital plan; in 2021 he signed a law ending cash bail, and in 2023 a ban on assault weapons and high-capacity magazines [[wikipedia]].

He was reelected over Darren Bailey in 2022, 54.9 to 42.4 percent [[wikipedia]]. His wealth drew scrutiny: after he appealed the assessment on a vacant mansion next to his home, the Cook County inspector general accused him of a scheme to cut his property taxes; he called it a political attack and repaid about $330,000 [[wikipedia]].

chapters.title: Trump's antagonist, and a third campaign
chapters.dek: Mass protests, the National Guard fight and $326 million of his own money.
chapters.body:
Pritzker built a national profile as a Trump opponent. In October 2023 he launched Think Big America to fund abortion-rights ballot campaigns in other states [[wikipedia]]. In an April 2025 speech in New Hampshire he said, "Never before in my life have I called for mass protests, for mobilization, for disruption, but I am now," urged Trump to "stop tearing down the Constitution in the name of my ancestors," and criticized "do-nothing" Democrats [[ap-nh-2025]].

In October 2025, during the immigration crackdown called Operation Midway Blitz, the administration federalized about 300 Illinois Guard members and sent 200 from Texas. Illinois and Chicago sued; Judge April Perry blocked the deployment on October 9, and Pritzker said "Donald Trump is not a king" [[tnd-guard-2025, cni-guard-2026]]. On December 23 the Supreme Court upheld her order 6–3, finding the administration "failed to identify a source of authority" for the military to execute the laws in Illinois; the troops left by mid-January [[cni-guard-2026]].

He announced a bid for a rare third term in June 2025 [[wikipedia]]. He gave $10 million to Illinois Future PAC to support his lieutenant governor, Juliana Stratton, in the Senate primary, and on August 10, 2026, put $65 million into his own campaign, bringing his self-funding across three races above $326 million [[fec-pritzker, suntimes-65m-2026]]. In September he disclosed that he has type 2 diabetes and has used a GLP-1 drug for two years [[wikipedia]]. In October he led Bailey by 20 points in one poll, called him "a bootlicker for Donald Trump," and was widely discussed as a 2028 presidential contender [[cni-third-term-2026]].
